title: The First Qubit
task: Can a quantum bit store information? Transform \( |0\rangle \) into \( |1\rangle \).
question: Can a quantum bit store information?
support: Start with the simplest possible quantum register: one qubit showing |0⟩. Can a gate make it carry a different value?
hints: There is only one gate available.
Use X to flip |0⟩ into |1⟩.

title: Undo The Change
task: Can a change be reversed? The qubit has already been flipped. Return it to \( |0\rangle \).
question: Can a change be reversed?
support: The circuit has already flipped the qubit. Instead of erasing the circuit, try to use another operation to retrace the change.
hints: The first X has already been placed.
X followed by X returns the qubit to its starting state.

title: Different Paths
task: Can extra moves cancel out? Reach \( |1\rangle \) from \( |0\rangle \) after adding more than one gate.
question: Can extra moves cancel out?
support: A circuit is not judged by how many gates it contains. Try making a longer route where part of the route erases itself.
hints: Build a route with more gates than the direct answer needs.
Two neighboring X gates cancel; the remaining X sets the final state.

title: Information Patterns
task: Can information move through multiple states? Transform \( |00\rangle \) into \( |11\rangle \).
question: Can information move through multiple states?
support: One qubit can change, but useful registers contain patterns. Can you transform both parts of the pattern without treating them as one big switch?
hints: Each qubit needs to change from 0 to 1.
Use one X on each qubit.

title: What Have We Learned?
task: What is a qubit really? Transform the information pattern \( |01\rangle \) into \( |10\rangle \).
question: What is a qubit really?
support: You have flipped, undone, canceled, and changed patterns. Use one final pattern change to name what the circuit has been acting on.
hints: Both qubits need to change.
Use X on each qubit to swap the pattern from |01⟩ to |10⟩.

title: Nothing Happened?
task: Can a quantum state change without changing its measurement? Use Z on \( |0\rangle \).
question: Can a quantum state change without changing its measurement?
support: So far, every useful change moved a visible 0 or 1. Try a gate whose action is real, even though this starting state still measures the same way.
hints: There is only one gate available.
Use Z and notice that this input hides the gate in the measured result.

title: The Invisible Difference
task: Apply Z to \( |1\rangle \). Did the physical state change, or only its vector representation?
question: Can two different vectors represent the same physical state?
support: Now try the same gate on |1⟩. The measured bit will not flip, but watch the state expression for a trace that was missing before.
hints: Use the same gate as before, but start from the state where its sign effect appears.
Z does not flip |1⟩ into |0⟩; it attaches a minus sign to |1⟩.

title: The Minus Sign
task: Why does a minus sign matter? Create the phase-flipped \( |-\rangle \) state.
question: Why does a minus sign matter?
support: A balanced state has two pieces. If only one piece receives the minus sign, the odds still look balanced, but the relationship between the pieces changes.
hints: You are already balanced between |0⟩ and |1⟩.
Use Z to change the relationship between the two pieces.

title: Hidden Information
task: Can information be stored in phase? Change \( |-\rangle \) back into \( |+\rangle \).
question: Can information be stored in phase?
support: The possible outcomes are unchanged. The puzzle is whether changing only the relationship between them can still count as changing information.
hints: The target restores the plus relationship between the two pieces.
Use the same gate again; phase changes can be reversible too.

title: What Did We Actually Discover?
task: What was changing all along? Turn the hidden change in \( |+\rangle \) into the visible state \( |1\rangle \).
question: What was changing all along?
support: You have changed values, signs, and relationships. Now build the reveal: make phase affect the measured bit.
hints: First create the phase relationship with Z.
Then use H to read that relationship as a definite bit value.

title: The Third State
task: Must a qubit always be 0 or 1? Create a state that is neither \( |0\rangle \) nor \( |1\rangle \).
question: Must a qubit always be 0 or 1?
support: You have changed qubits between 0 and 1, and you have seen hidden phase. Now try making a state that does not look like either classical option.
hints: There is only one gate available.
Use the gate and watch the probability bars split evenly.

title: Fifty Fifty
task: What outcome will appear when we measure a superposition? Create a state with equal probability of \( |0\rangle \) and \( |1\rangle \).
question: What outcome will appear when we measure a superposition?
support: A qubit can hold more than one possibility before measurement. Make a state where neither outcome has all the probability.
hints: Start from |1⟩ and use the only available gate.
The goal is equal probabilities, not a single certain outcome.

title: Precise, Not Random
task: If measurement is uncertain, is the state just random? Turn \( |+\rangle \) back into \( |0\rangle \).
question: If measurement is uncertain, is the state just random?
support: A balanced state can look like a coin toss when measured. Test whether it is still a precise state that a gate can control.
hints: Use the gate that created |+⟩ from |0⟩.
The same operation can also turn |+⟩ back into |0⟩.

title: Build The Balance
task: Can we prepare uncertainty on purpose? Transform \( |1\rangle \) into the balanced \( |+\rangle \) state.
question: Can we prepare uncertainty on purpose?
support: Superposition is not something that only happens by accident. Set up the input, then create the balanced state deliberately.
hints: Using H immediately from |1⟩ gives the wrong balanced state.
First flip |1⟩ to |0⟩, then create |+⟩.

title: What Is Superposition?
task: Can superposition be placed on one qubit inside a larger register? Transform \( |10\rangle \) into \( |+0\rangle \).
question: Can only one qubit become superposed?
support: A register can contain more than one qubit. Prepare the register, then place superposition only where it is needed.
hints: The second qubit should stay 0 in the final state.
First change |10⟩ to |00⟩, then apply H only to the first qubit.

title: Phase Is Hidden
task: Can something change without changing what we measure? Transform \( |+\rangle \) into \( |-\rangle \).
question: Can something change without changing what we measure?
support: You have seen this kind of hidden change before. Make the same 50/50 state carry the opposite phase so the next puzzles can reveal it.
hints: The two states have the same probabilities. Look for a gate that changes a sign, not a bit value.
Z leaves |0⟩ unchanged and gives |1⟩ a minus sign.

title: HZH = X
task: Can a phase flip become a bit flip? Starting from \( |0\rangle \), reach \( |1\rangle \) using only H and Z.
question: Can a phase flip become a bit flip?
support: Z only changes phase, so it should not flip |0⟩ into |1⟩ directly. But what if you change the basis before and after the phase flip?
hints: Use H to move from the computational basis into the plus/minus basis.
Try placing Z between two H gates.

title: HXH = Z
task: Can a bit flip become a phase flip? Starting from \( |+\rangle \), reach \( |-\rangle \) using only H and X.
question: Can a bit flip become a phase flip?
support: X is a bit flip in the normal |0⟩/|1⟩ basis. But in a different basis, the same operation can change phase instead.
hints: Use H to change basis before applying X.
Mirror the previous pattern: H, then X, then H.

title: Make Zero Impossible
task: The first H is already placed. Complete the circuit so \( P(|0\rangle)=0 \).
question: Can you completely eliminate one outcome?
support: The pre-built H has created two possible paths. Can you arrange them so the |0⟩ outcome cancels away completely?
hints: The pre-built H already created |+⟩. First change it into |−⟩.
After creating |-⟩, use H to turn cancellation into a visible |1⟩ outcome.

title: What Is Interference?
task: The circuit already created and phase-marked two paths. Add the final gate that turns the hidden phase into \( |1\rangle \).
question: What have we actually discovered?
support: The pre-built H→Z has prepared |−⟩. One final basis change can make that hidden phase show up as a visible measurement result.
hints: The pre-built gates already created |−⟩.
Use H to recombine the paths and reveal the phase as |1⟩.

title: Together
task: Can two qubits be prepared together? Transform \( |00\rangle \) into \( |11\rangle \).
question: Can two qubits be prepared together?
support: So far, one qubit has carried the story. Now there are two. Can you prepare a state that describes both qubits at once?
hints: Both qubits need to change from 0 to 1.
Use one X on each qubit.

title: Connected
task: Can changing one qubit affect another? Use the controlled operation to transform \( |10\rangle \) into \( |11\rangle \).
question: Can changing one qubit affect another?
support: One qubit is already active. Can it act as a condition that changes the other qubit?
hints: Kets are written |Q1 Q0⟩, so in |10⟩, Q1=1 and Q0=0. Use Q1 as the control.
CNOT(Q1→Q0) flips Q0 because control Q1 is 1.

title: The Bell State
task: Can two qubits become one quantum system? Transform \( |00\rangle \) into Bell State \( \Phi^+ \).
question: Can two qubits become one quantum system?
support: A superposition can hold more than one possibility. A controlled operation can connect qubits. What happens when those ideas meet?
hints: First create a split possibility on q0.
Then connect q1 to q0 with CX.

title: More Than Correlation
task: Why is entanglement special? Create a Bell state from \( |10\rangle \).
question: Why is entanglement special?
support: Ordinary correlation says two values match. Entanglement is deeper: the whole pair has a state that cannot be assigned to each qubit separately.
hints: Start by splitting the first qubit into two possibilities.
Then use CX to connect the second qubit to those possibilities.

title: What Is Entanglement?
task: What have we actually discovered? Prepare the entangled state \( (|00\rangle - |11\rangle)/\sqrt{2} \).
question: What have we actually discovered?
support: You have seen two qubits act as one shared system. Prepare one more entangled state and focus on what cannot be described separately.
hints: Begin with q1 set to 1.
Create a split possibility on q0, then connect the qubits with CX.

title: The Control Qubit
task: Can one qubit decide what happens to another? Use CX to transform \( |01\rangle \) into \( |11\rangle \).
question: Can one qubit decide what happens to another?
support: A two-qubit circuit can contain a decision: one qubit can determine whether another qubit changes.
hints: The active qubit should control the other one.
Use CX so the second qubit changes only when the control is active.

title: Conditional Action
task: Can the same gate behave differently depending on the input? Use CX on \( |00\rangle \).
question: Can the same gate behave differently depending on the input?
support: A controlled operation does not always visibly change the bits. Its effect depends on the information already present.
hints: There is only one gate available.
Use CX and notice that the state can stay the same for a meaningful reason.

title: Information Transfer
task: Can information be transferred between qubits? Create information on one qubit, then propagate it to the other.
question: Can information be transferred between qubits?
support: A circuit can create information on one qubit and then let that information affect another qubit.
hints: First create an active control.
Then use CX to pass that information to the other qubit.

title: Swap Places
task: Can two qubits exchange their information? Build a reusable SWAP circuit using only CX. It should swap any two-qubit input, including \( |10\rangle \rightarrow |01\rangle \).
question: Can two qubits exchange their information?
support: A shortcut can solve one displayed input. A true SWAP circuit must exchange the two qubits for every possible input.
hints: Do not only solve |10⟩ → |01⟩. Build the operation that swaps both qubits for any input.
A full SWAP uses three CX gates: one direction, the other direction, then the first direction again.

title: Information Flow
task: What have we actually learned? Create information on either qubit, then route it across the two-qubit system with the three-CX pattern.
question: What have we actually learned?
support: Controlled operations can move, redirect, and reshape information. Build a small circuit where information is created, then routed to the other qubit.
hints: First create information with X on either qubit.
Then use the three-CX routing pattern to move that information to the other qubit. The mirrored direction is valid too.

title: Three Qubits
task: What changes when we add a third qubit? Prepare the full-register outcome \( |111\rangle \).
question: What changes when we add a third qubit?
support: A third qubit widens the state label. Start simply: prepare one complete three-qubit outcome and read it as a whole register pattern.
hints: Each inactive qubit needs the same simple change.
Use X on all three wires.

title: Shared Information
task: Can one part of a register constrain all the others? Prepare the globally consistent outcome \( |111\rangle \).
question: Can one part of a register constrain all the others?
support: A three-qubit register can be prepared so every observed part agrees with the whole outcome. If one part is 1, the complete pattern is fixed here.
hints: Q0 is already fixed as the active part of the register.
Use CX from Q0 to each other qubit so the whole register ends in one consistent pattern.

title: All Together
task: Can three qubits become one globally constrained system? Prepare \( (|000\rangle + |111\rangle)/\sqrt{2} \).
question: Can three qubits become one globally constrained system?
support: The register may have local uncertainty while still allowing only globally consistent outcomes. Try preparing a state with only |000⟩ and |111⟩ present.
hints: Start by creating a split possibility on one qubit.
Use controlled operations so only the full-register outcomes |000⟩ and |111⟩ remain possible.

title: Beyond Bell States
task: Why is a GHZ state not explained by pairs? Prepare \( (|000\rangle + |111\rangle)/\sqrt{2} \).
question: Why is a GHZ state not explained by pairs?
support: Pairwise thinking is not enough here. The important object is the complete three-qubit register and its allowed global outcomes.
hints: Create a superposition first.
Then use control so the complete register has only the alternatives |000⟩ and |111⟩.

title: One System, Three Qubits
task: A GHZ state has already been prepared: \( (|000\rangle + |111\rangle)/\sqrt{2} \). What does this state mean?
question: What have we actually discovered?
concept: This time the circuit construction is finished. Focus on the state itself: a GHZ state is a rule over the whole register, not a pattern to build again.
support: The register is already in a GHZ state. The question is not which gate comes next, but which full-register outcomes the state allows.
hints: Read the state as a statement about complete register outcomes.
Only |000⟩ and |111⟩ have non-zero amplitude in this GHZ state.

title: Hidden Mark
task: Use one controlled phase operation on \( |+\rangle|1\rangle \). The visible bit probabilities should stay the same, but the control should receive a phase mark.
question: Can a controlled operation mark a state invisibly?
support: The target is fixed at |1⟩. Apply a controlled phase operation and look for a change that does not appear as a visible bit flip.
hints: Use the controlled phase gate.
The target remains |1⟩; the control receives the phase mark.

title: Control Affects Control
task: Use one CX on \( |1\rangle|−\rangle \). Interpret the resulting minus sign before the control is put into superposition.
question: Can the target setup affect the control logic?
support: The target is prepared as |−⟩. Apply CX and notice that the conditional flip does not show up as an ordinary target bit change.
hints: Use CX with q0 as control and q1 as target.
The target is |−⟩, so a conditional flip becomes a phase effect.

title: Unexpected Phase Change
task: Use one CX on \( |+\rangle|−\rangle \). The target is acted on, but the control should become \( |−\rangle \).
question: Why did the qubit that was not targeted change?
support: The controlled gate targets q1, but the phase-sensitive target can kick information back onto q0. Watch which qubit carries the phase after the operation.
hints: Use CX with q0 as control and q1 as target.
The target remains |−⟩, while q0 changes from |+⟩ to |−⟩.

title: Setup Matters
task: Use the same CX circuit on \( |+\rangle|+\rangle \). This time the target setup should prevent phase kickback.
question: Does every target state create kickback?
support: Use the same controlled operation as before, but with the target prepared as |+⟩ instead of |−⟩. The circuit is the same; the setup changes the result.
hints: Use CX with q0 as control and q1 as target, just like the previous level.
Because the target is |+⟩, the same gate does not create a kicked-back phase.

title: Compute, Encode, Reveal
task: Kick phase back onto the control with CX, then use H on the control to reveal the stored phase as \( |1\rangle \).
question: How does hidden phase become a useful answer?
support: First use controlled logic to write information into phase. Only after that should interference reveal the stored phase as a visible bit.
hints: First use CX with q0 as control and q1 as target.
Then apply H to q0 to reveal |−⟩ as |1⟩.

title: Oracle Intuition
task: Can a hidden rule classify one input differently from the others? Query the rule on \( |++\rangle \).
question: Can a circuit behave like a hidden rule?
support: An oracle is a black-box function. It receives possible inputs and classifies each one as valid or invalid without directly announcing the answer.
hints: Look for the operation that classifies only the input |11⟩ as valid.
The goal is not to read the answer. It is to apply the hidden rule once.

title: Simple Marking Rule
task: Can a rule mark one valid input without directly revealing it? Query the rule that accepts \( |1\rangle \).
question: Can a rule identify validity without showing the answer?
support: A classical question asks for the answer. An oracle query applies a rule and only labels whether an input is valid.
hints: Apply the operation that labels |1⟩ as the accepted input.
Do not look for a measurement result. Look for rule-based classification.

title: Hidden Structure Effect
task: Can a hidden rule classify \( |10\rangle \) as valid while the other inputs remain invalid?
question: Can hidden structure exist before the answer is visible?
support: The oracle applies a function to the input space. It can classify one input as valid even when direct reading has not revealed which input matters.
hints: Think of the oracle as the rule f(10)=1.
The other inputs should remain in the unmarked class.

title: Why Classical Fails
task: Why is a rule query not the same as checking each answer manually? Query the hidden rule that accepts \( |01\rangle \).
question: Why is brute-force inspection the wrong model?
support: Classical inspection asks one candidate at a time. Oracle thinking treats the circuit as a black-box function that can be queried as a whole.
hints: Treat |01⟩ as the only input for which f(x)=1.
The goal is a rule query, not a list of tested candidates.

title: Oracle as Computation Primitive
task: What have we actually built? Query a reusable oracle whose hidden rule accepts \( |00\rangle \).
question: What is an oracle for?
support: An oracle is not the whole algorithm. It is the reusable part that encodes the problem as a hidden function.
hints: Think of the function table: f(00)=1 and every other input maps to 0.
Build the reusable query, not a direct answer display.

title: Why Marking Is Not Enough
task: A valid state is known, but every outcome is still equally likely. Keep \( |11\rangle \) no more likely than the others.
question: Why is knowing the valid state not enough?
support: A valid answer can be identified without becoming easier to observe. If all probabilities stay equal, knowing validity has not changed the distribution.
hints: Focus on the measurement chances, not on naming the valid state.
For this step, the valid state should remain equally likely.

title: First Sign of Bias
task: Can a balanced distribution become uneven? Shift \( |++\rangle \) so only two outcomes remain likely.
question: Can a balanced distribution become uneven?
support: Before amplification feels useful, the learner needs to see a smaller move: probability does not have to stay spread evenly across every candidate.
hints: Aim for two likely outcomes instead of four equal ones.
The final distribution should be biased, not guaranteed.

title: Reinforcement of Probability
task: Can a valid state become more likely without becoming certain? Bias the distribution toward \( |11\rangle \).
question: Can a valid state become more likely without becoming certain?
support: Start with every candidate equally likely. The task is only to make |11⟩ more likely than it was before, not to force it as the guaranteed outcome.
hints: |11⟩ should become more likely than before, but it should not be the only possible result.
Aim for a weak bias shared with one other outcome.

title: Bias Becomes Amplification
task: A weak bias toward \( |11\rangle \) already exists. Which description correctly turns that bias into amplification?
question: How does a small bias become an amplification pattern?
concept: Read the probability change: amplification means a weak preference becomes stronger without becoming a guaranteed selection.
support: Level 48 created the first weak preference. This checkpoint asks what should happen next at the probability level only.
hints: Compare before and after probabilities.
The correct answer strengthens the bias without claiming certainty.

title: Amplification as Computational Advantage
task: What is the final Chapter 10 takeaway about amplitude amplification?
question: What does amplification contribute to search?
concept: Use the probability model only: weak bias can become stronger bias, and stronger bias makes the valid answer more likely to be observed.
support: Bring the chapter together: amplification is useful because probability can be shifted toward the valid state without treating the result as guaranteed.
hints: Choose the answer that stays at the probability level.
The correct idea is stronger likelihood, not certainty.

title: Why One Step Is Not Enough
task: One oracle plus amplification pass improves the chance of success. Why might that still not be enough?
question: Why is one improvement not always enough?
concept: Chapter 11 starts above the mechanics. Treat oracle and amplification as abstract steps: one identifies valid states, the other improves their likelihood.
support: A single pass can make the valid answer more likely, but a small improvement may still leave too much probability on other candidates.
hints: Do not look for certainty.
Compare a small improvement with a high chance of success.

title: Iteration Idea
task: What is the new idea when the oracle plus amplification pattern is repeated?
question: What does repetition add?
concept: Iteration means using the same abstract pattern again so an existing advantage can become stronger.
support: The chapter shift is not a new operation. The shift is using known abstractions repeatedly to improve success likelihood.
hints: Think about likelihood across rounds.
The repeated pattern should strengthen the same valid region.

title: Convergence Toward Solution
task: What should happen to the probability distribution across useful repeated rounds?
question: What trend should the loop create?
concept: Convergence means the distribution trends toward the valid answer as the abstract loop is applied carefully: flat at first, then slightly lifted, then visibly biased.
support: The learner should track the shape of the probability distribution, not a low-level implementation.
hints: Look for a trend, not a single guaranteed jump.
The valid answer should become more likely over useful rounds.

title: Classical vs Quantum Iteration
task: Why is this loop idea different from simply guessing again?
question: Why is repeated guessing not the same idea?
concept: Classical repetition retries. Grover-style iteration is different at the abstraction level because it reshapes the probability distribution.
support: A repeated guess samples again from the same situation. A useful Grover-style loop changes the distribution before the next observation.
hints: Compare retrying with reshaping likelihood.
The correct answer changes the distribution before measuring.

title: Applying Iteration Thinking to Structured Problems
task: How can iteration thinking help with structured selection problems?
question: Can the loop idea transfer?
concept: Use the whole chapter as a reasoning tool: a weak preference can become useful when a structured process reinforces it repeatedly.
support: The goal is not to build a mechanism. The goal is to recognize when repeated refinement can narrow a structured set of choices.
hints: Think about a candidate set, not a construction.
Look for weak preference becoming stronger through repeated refinement.

title: The Full Picture Appears
task: What is the best high-level description of a quantum algorithm at this point in Qubit Quest?
question: What has the pattern become?
concept: Chapter 12 is a unification layer. It does not add a new concept; it connects the abstract roles learned across the last three chapters.
support: The learner now steps back from individual ideas and sees the algorithm as a structured process rather than a single clever trick.
hints: Look for the answer that combines roles into one process.
Do not reduce the chapter to one isolated step.

title: Separation of Roles
task: How should the oracle, amplification, and iteration roles be separated conceptually?
question: Which part does what?
concept: Each role has a distinct job in the abstract model: define what counts, make valid outcomes more likely, and repeat the pattern.
support: The goal is clean role separation. The learner should not blur definition, likelihood increase, and repetition into one vague idea.
hints: One role defines validity.
Another role changes likelihood, and iteration organizes repeated use.

title: Why Composition Matters
task: Why does computational advantage depend on combining the roles rather than naming them separately?
question: Why is combination useful?
concept: A role by itself is only part of the story. The useful model is compositional: definition, bias, and repetition work as a layered process.
support: The learner now asks why separate abstractions become more powerful when they are arranged together.
hints: A definition alone does not create the full advantage.
A likelihood change becomes more useful when organized by repeated structure.

title: Classical vs Quantum Structure
task: At this meta level, what structural difference separates ordinary repeated search from the quantum algorithm model?
question: What is structurally different?
concept: Classical repeated search tries again. The quantum structure discussed here organizes a probability-shaping process around valid solutions.
support: The comparison is not about implementation. It is about whether repetition merely retries or whether it is part of a structured probability-shaping system.
hints: Classical repetition retries or checks.
The quantum model uses a structured probability-shaping process.

title: Unified Quantum Algorithm Model
task: Which abstract pipeline best summarizes Chapters 9-12 together?
question: What is the unified model?
concept: The synthesis is a layered abstract pipeline: define what counts as valid, bias probability toward validity, then iterate the structure.
support: The learner should leave the chapter with a portable algorithm model, not a construction recipe.
hints: Look for a three-layer pipeline.
The correct answer stays conceptual: define, bias, iterate.

title: Different Vectors, Same Qubit
question: Which statement is physically correct?
hints: Ask whether the factor changes one amplitude relative to another or multiplies the entire vector.
legacyTask: Compare \( |1\rangle \), \( -|1\rangle \), and \( i|1\rangle \). Which statement is physically correct?

title: Uncompute the Hidden Turn
task: The fixed H → S → Z prefix prepared \( |-i\rangle \) from \( |0\rangle \). Append the inverse continuation that restores \( |0\rangle \).
concept: The fixed prefix is part of the evidence. Work backward through what it did; the order of the undoing matters.
hints: Undo the relative phase before undoing the superposition.
For this state, S cancels the accumulated relative phase; then H returns |+⟩ to |0⟩.
legacyTask: The fixed H → S → Z prefix prepared \( |-i\rangle \) from \( |0\rangle \). Append the inverse continuation that restores \( |0\rangle \).

title: Same Data, Different Qubit
question: What does the additional X-basis evidence establish?
intro: Three preparations share the same ideal Z-basis histogram.
helper: The third preparation randomly chooses \(|0\rangle\) or \(|1\rangle\).
hints: The ensemble is a classical random preparation, not a coherent sum of amplitudes.
legacyTask:
Ideal evidence:

In the Z basis, |+⟩, |−⟩, and an ensemble where half the preparations are |0⟩ and half are |1⟩ all give P(0)=1/2 and P(1)=1/2.

In the X basis, |+⟩ always gives +, |−⟩ always gives −, while the random |0⟩/|1⟩ ensemble remains 50/50. What does this establish?

title: Which Wire Controls the Change?
question: Which control/target topology fits both cases?
intro: One fixed CNOT produced both mappings.
helper: Wires: q0, q1, q2 top-to-bottom. Kets: |q2 q1 q0⟩.
hints: Compare which ket bit changed in the second mapping, then test the proposed control against both inputs.
legacyTask:
Wires run q0, q1, q2 from top to bottom; kets read |q2 q1 q0⟩. One fixed CNOT produced both mappings:

|010⟩ → |010⟩
|100⟩ → |101⟩

Which topology fits both?

title: The Bell Decoder Bug
question: Which repair and resulting basis output are correct?
intro: This proposed Bell decoder does not produce a basis state.
hints: A decoder applies the inverse of the preparation sequence.
legacyTask:
Input: |Φ+⟩=(|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2.

A proposed decoder applies H(q0), then CNOT(control q0, target q1), but its output is not a basis state. Which repair and output are correct?

evidence.label: PROPOSED DECODER
evidence.content: Proposed decoder: H on q0, followed by CNOT with q0 control and q1 target.

title: When Does Kickback Happen?
question: Which input creates an observable phase change on the control while leaving the target state unchanged?
helper: The first state in each option is the control.
hints: Look for a target that returns an eigenvalue −1 and a control with two coherent branches.
legacyTask: A controlled-X uses the first state as control and the second as target. Which input creates a useful, observable phase change on the control while leaving the target state unchanged?

evidence.label: CONTROLLED OPERATION
evidence.content: Controlled X with q0 as control and q1 as target.

title: Which State Did the Oracle Mark?
question: Which marked state and oracle structure match the evidence?
intro: A phase oracle changes one sign in a uniform state.
helper: Wires: q0 above q1. Kets: |q1 q0⟩.
hints: The negative amplitude identifies the marked ket. An X wrapper makes CZ trigger when that wrapped qubit was initially 0.
legacyTask:
